messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 77
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Delivery Driver
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 48

# Vignette: Harold

Harold is a 77-year-old married man who has spent the better part of the last decade behind the wheel of a delivery truck, a job he took up after retiring from a longer career in warehouse management. He liked the solitude of it, the rhythm of the routes, the small talk with customers at their doors. It kept him moving, kept him useful. That is how he has always defined himself — as a man who shows up, who does the work, who doesn't complain.

Fourteen months ago, Harold was making an evening delivery to an apartment complex on the edge of town when two men approached him from behind a dumpster. What followed happened quickly — a demand for his keys and wallet, a shove that sent him hard into the side of his truck, and then a sustained beating when he didn't move fast enough. He remembers the sound of his own ribs cracking. He remembers the pavement against his cheek and the smell of motor oil and the strange, detached thought that he should try to memorize their faces. He lay there for nearly twenty minutes before a resident found him.

His physical injuries healed over the following months — the broken ribs, the laceration above his eye, the bruised kidney. His wife, Donna, nursed him through those weeks with the steady patience she has always brought to their fifty-one years of marriage. Harold told her he was fine. He told himself the same thing.

But something did not heal with the rest of him. The first time he tried to return to his route, he sat in the truck in the company parking lot for forty minutes and could not make himself pull out onto the street. He told his dispatcher he had a stomach bug. He tried again the following week and made it as far as the apartment complex before his hands began shaking so badly he had to pull over. He has not driven that route since.

Now Harold sleeps in fragments, waking between two and four in the morning with his heart hammering and the absolute certainty that someone is in the house. He gets up and checks the locks — the front door, the back door, the garage — sometimes twice, sometimes three times, before he can sit down again. Donna has started sleeping with the bedroom light on because she noticed he panics in the dark. He hasn't told her why, exactly. He doesn't want her to think he has become someone who is afraid.

During the day, Harold finds it hard to sit still, but also hard to do much of anything purposeful. He watches television without following it. He stopped going to the diner where he and his friend Ray have eaten breakfast on Thursdays for fifteen years, because it means parking in a lot and walking across open space, and his body will not stop cataloguing every person nearby, every shadow, every sound that doesn't fit. Ray has called several times. Harold hasn't called back.

He is irritable in ways that trouble him — short with Donna over nothing, then flooded with shame about it afterward. He describes himself as "not right in the head," and says it the way a man of his generation says such things: quietly, with considerable reluctance, and only after being asked directly. He does not understand why the fear has not simply faded the way he expected it to. He is a man who survived decades of physical labor, who raised three children, who once drove through a blizzard to make a delivery because he had made a commitment. Being ambushed in a parking lot should not have broken something this fundamental.

What troubles Harold most, sitting across from his therapist with his hands folded in his lap, is not the nightmares or the locked doors or even the lost Thursday breakfasts. It is the truck, still sitting in the company lot, and the routes he knows by heart, and the quiet purpose they once gave him — all of it waiting just beyond a line he cannot yet find a way to cross.
